title: The Backyard Shed Where Momofuku Ando Started Again at 48
dek: After a credit union's collapse took nearly everything he owned in 1957, Momofuku Ando spent a year alone in a garden shed working out instant noodles.

story.event: Inventing Chicken Ramen in a backyard shed after a credit union's bankruptcy
story.summary: In 1957 a credit union where Momofuku Ando was a director went bankrupt and he gave up his assets to cover its debts, keeping only a rented house in Ikeda, near Osaka. He spent a year alone in a shed behind the house, an amateur at noodle-making, until flash-frying noodles in oil, an idea taken from his wife's tempura, let them keep and soften again in hot water. Chicken Ramen, the first instant noodles, went on sale on 25 August 1958.
paragraphs: In 1957, at the age of 47, Momofuku Ando lost almost everything he owned. A credit union where he served as a director went bankrupt, and he gave up his own assets to meet its debts. What remained, by his company's account, was a rented house in Ikeda, near Osaka. One history says he had taken the post at a friend's request, and that he later recalled bitter regret at entering finance, a field he knew little about.

He did have an idea he had carried since the hungry years after the war, when he had seen a long queue at a black-market ramen stall near Osaka Station and wondered why the authorities were promoting bread made from American wheat rather than the noodles people were queuing for. With no business left to run, he built a shed of about ten square metres behind the house and set out to make ramen that could be ready at home with nothing but hot water. He was an amateur at noodle-making. He set himself five tests: the noodles had to taste good enough not to tire of, keep in a kitchen, be quick to prepare, cost little and be safe.

For a year he worked there alone, according to his company without a single day off and on about four hours' sleep a night, throwing away trial after trial. The hard problems were drying noodles so they would store and making them soft again in hot water. The answer came from his wife Masako's cooking: watching her fry tempura, he saw hot oil drive water out of the batter. Flash-fried, his seasoned noodles dried out and were left full of tiny holes that hot water could fill again.

Chicken Ramen went on sale on 25 August 1958, when Ando was 48. It cost ¥35 a serving when a bundle of udon cost ¥6, and wholesalers were at first reluctant to stock it; by the company's account, orders soon swamped them. The Economist later reported 13 million bags sold in the first year. Cup Noodles followed in 1971. Ando died in January 2007, aged 96, and by the Economist's account still ate Chicken Ramen almost every day.

quote.text: Solon was under a delusion when he said that a man when he grows old may learn many things—for he can no more learn much than he can run much; youth is the time for any extraordinary toil.
quote.source_title: The Republic, tr. Benjamin Jowett, Project Gutenberg eBook #1497
quote.connection: Socrates, planning the education of his ideal city's rulers, holds that heavy new learning belongs to the young. Ando, an amateur at 48, learned a new craft alone in a year. He also paid for it in sleep, so Socrates' point about the cost of such toil is not simply refuted.

reflection: It is easy to read this as a story about never being too old, and partly it is. Ando started from almost nothing at 47, in a craft where he was a beginner, and made something people still eat every day.

But Socrates was not foolish to think that great toil weighs differently at different ages, and a year on four hours' sleep is not a method to copy. What seems worth keeping is narrower: before he began, Ando set himself five plain tests, and every failed batch could be judged against them. Whatever you are learning late, or learning again, a short list of what good looks like may carry you further than longer nights would.
invitation: Choose one thing you are still learning, at work or outside it, and write down the three plain tests a good result would have to pass. Leave the note where you will see it tomorrow, and stop at a sensible hour tonight.

cross_checks.claim: In 1957 a credit union in which Ando held a senior post went bankrupt and he lost nearly all his assets
He spent about a year working alone in a shed behind his house, with little sleep and no days off
Flash-frying the noodles in oil, the idea taken from his wife's tempura, solved drying and rehydration
Chicken Ramen went on sale in August 1958 (25 August by the company's date)
It cost roughly six times as much as ordinary noodles (¥35 against ¥6 for udon)

research_notes: Ando's role in the credit union differs by source: Nissin's own history says he was 'working as a director'; AFP (Mail & Guardian, Taipei Times) says managing director; Nippon.com says he headed it at a friend's request; the Economist says he 'presided over a credit association'. The story uses the company's conservative 'served as a director' and attributes the friend's request to 'one history' (Nippon.com). What he kept: Nissin says a rented house in Ikeda, Nippon.com 'a rental property in Ikeda'. The black-market noodle queue: Nissin and Nippon.com place it in the postwar food shortage near Osaka Station; the Economist places a similar sight in 1957 on his walk home from a salt works. The story follows the company and Nippon.com and does not date the queue precisely. 'Cheered himself up with the thought that all he had lost was property' is Nissin's account of his thinking and is attributed to the company. Price: Nissin gives ¥35 a serving against ¥6 for a bundle of udon; the Economist says six times the price of fresh noodles; consistent. Sales: the only first-year figure found is the Economist's 13 million bags, so it is attributed; Nippon.com gives ¥4.3 billion in yearly sales five years after launch, not used. Age: born 5 March 1910 (AFP, Nissin), so 47 at the 1957 bankruptcy and 48 at the August 1958 launch, which matches Nippon.com's 'already 48'. Nippon.com also mentions wartime and postwar arrests (black-market diversion; tax evasion) of which it says he was found innocent and released; the Economist mentions jail over a scholarship scheme. These are outside the episode and are left out. The company was founded in 1948 (AFP) and the story names it only as his company. The Plato passage is Socrates arguing, in the design of the guardians' education, that the hardest study should come in youth; it is applied here by analogy.
